tasks.title: Array capacity and fault tolerance
tasks.statement: Write a function raid_summary(level, sizes, spares). level is one of the strings raid0, raid1, raid5, raid6, raid10; sizes are the sizes of the working disks in gigabytes, spares are the sizes of the spare disks. Rules of this task: an array uses the size of the smallest working disk for every member; the minimum number of working disks is raid0: 2, raid1: 2, raid5: 3, raid6: 4, raid10: 2 (raid10 here is md raid10 with two copies, which also works with an odd number of disks). Usable capacity: raid0 is n*m, raid1 is m, raid5 is (n-1)*m, raid6 is (n-2)*m, raid10 is n*m//2 (integer division), where n is the number of working disks and m is the smallest of them. Failures survived for sure: raid0 0, raid1 n-1, raid5 1, raid6 2, raid10 1; in the best case (when the failed disks happen to be placed well): raid0 0, raid1 n-1, raid5 1, raid6 2, raid10 n//2. A spare is usable only if its size is at least m. Return a tuple (capacity, guaranteed, best case, number of usable spares). For an unknown level or too few disks return None.
tasks.hint: Check the minimum number of disks first, then m = min(sizes) and a branch per level; count the spares with a generator using s >= m.

tasks.title: Degraded arrays in /proc/mdstat
tasks.statement: Write a function degraded_arrays(text): text is the content of /proc/mdstat. An array block starts with a line "name : state level members..." at the first character, followed by indented lines; the Personalities and unused devices lines are not blocks. A member is written like sdb1[0], and a (F) mark in parentheses (it may stand together with other letters, for example (SF)) means a failed disk. An array counts as a problem when it has a pair [n/m] with m < n (on the status line, for example [4/3] [UUU_]) or when it is inactive; raid0 has no [n/m] pair, so such an array is skipped (unless it is inactive). For every problem array return a tuple (name, how many disks are missing n-m or None for inactive, a sorted list of the names of failed disks without role numbers, action, percent, estimated finish in minutes). The action is one of the words resync, recovery, reshape, check, repair when the block has a fragment like "recovery = 12.6%" (any amount of spaces around =; the percent is a number with a dot, return it as a float); if there is no such fragment (for example resync=PENDING), the action, percent and estimate are None. The estimate is the number from finish=127.5min as a float, or None if there is no such fragment. Sort the result by array name as plain strings.
tasks.hint: Cut the text into blocks at the lines that start with "name : "; inside a block use regular expressions for [n/m], (F) on members and "(resync|recovery|...) = N%".

tasks.title: Replacing a failed disk step by step
tasks.statement: Simulate a simplified md array. The function replace_sequence(level, n, devices, spares, commands): level is raid1, raid5 or raid6, n is the number of slots of the array, devices are the names of the working disks, spares are the names of the spare disks, commands is a list of command strings. The number of working disks needed for the data to be intact is raid1: 1, raid5: n-1, raid6: n-2. A disk can be in one of four lists: active (in sync), rebuilding, spare, failed (marked as failed but still listed in the array). Commands: "fail X" moves a disk from active, rebuilding or spare to failed; if it was active or rebuilding and there are spares, and at least the needed number of disks remain in active, the first spare (in order) at once moves to rebuilding; an unknown disk is rejected. "remove X" removes a disk that is currently in failed or spare; otherwise (active, rebuilding or unknown) the command is rejected. "add X": if the name is already in any list (including failed) the command is rejected; otherwise, if a slot is free (active + rebuilding < n) and active holds at least the needed number of disks, the disk becomes rebuilding, and if not it becomes spare. "done" (no argument) makes all rebuilding disks active if active holds at least the needed number of disks; in every other case (including nothing being rebuilt) it does nothing and is not rejected. Any other command is rejected. After all commands return a tuple (state, number of active, number of spare, number of failed, number of rejected commands). The state is "FAILED" if active is below the needed number; otherwise "clean", with ", degraded" appended when active < n and then ", recovering" if something is rebuilding.
tasks.hint: Keep four lists and a rejected counter; parse each command with split(); after fail start a spare only if active >= the needed number.

tasks.title: Parsing mdadm --detail
tasks.statement: Write a function detail_report(text): text is the output of mdadm --detail. Return a dictionary with the keys level (the value of the Raid Level field, for example raid5), state (the value of the State field without surrounding spaces), active, missing, faulty, rebuilding, spares (sorted lists) and progress. The lines before the table look like "Field : value" with padding spaces. The table starts at the line with the headings Number Major Minor RaidDevice State; in each table row the fields are separated by spaces: number, major, minor, slot number RaidDevice (or "-"), then state words and finally the device path (it may be absent). The state words (check in this order) define the category: removed means an empty slot (the slot number goes into missing as an int), faulty puts the path into faulty, rebuilding into rebuilding, spare into spares, active into active. Ignore the other words (sync, writemostly, set-A and so on); skip table rows with fewer than five fields and empty lines. progress is the integer percentage from a line like "Rebuild Status : 42% complete" (the same for Resync, Reshape and Check), or None if there is no such line.
tasks.hint: Match fields before the table with a regular expression like ^(Raid Level|State)\s*:\s*(.*)$; after the Number ... RaidDevice line switch to table mode and split the rows.

tasks.title: Triage of a SMART attribute table
tasks.statement: Write a function smart_triage(text): text is the output of smartctl -A. An attribute row is a line with at least ten words whose first word consists of digits; ignore the other lines (headings, empty ones). The fields in order are ID#, ATTRIBUTE_NAME, FLAG, VALUE, WORST, THRESH, TYPE, UPDATED, WHEN_FAILED, and the rest is RAW_VALUE; you need only the ID, WHEN_FAILED and the first integer in RAW_VALUE (for example 31 in "31 (Min/Max 22/46)"). Rules. An attribute is "failing now" when WHEN_FAILED is FAILING_NOW. An attribute is "suspicious" in one of these cases: WHEN_FAILED is In_the_past; the ID is one of 5, 197, 198 and the raw value is greater than zero; the ID is one of 190, 194 and the raw value is at least 55. Return a tuple (verdict, list of IDs). The verdict is FAIL if there is at least one failing-now attribute; then the list holds the sorted IDs of the failing-now ones. Otherwise WARN if there are suspicious ones; then the list holds their sorted IDs without repeats. Otherwise the tuple ('OK', []).
tasks.hint: Test a row with len(t) >= 10 and t[0].isdigit(); the raw value is re.match(r'\d+', t[9]).

tasks.title: Alerts from the NVMe SMART block
tasks.statement: Write a function nvme_alerts(text): text is the output of smartctl -a for an NVMe disk. You care about lines like "Field:   value"; split each line at the first colon and squeeze several spaces in the field name into one (the real output has "Warning  Comp. Temperature Time" with two spaces). Numbers may contain comma separators, a % sign and notes after the number ("12,345 [6.32 TB]"): take the leading part of digits and commas. The Critical Warning field is a hexadecimal number like 0x04; its bits are 0: spare, 1: temperature, 2: reliability, 3: read_only, 4: volatile_backup; for every set bit add an alert "critical:<name>". In addition: "spare_low" if Available Spare is strictly less than Available Spare Threshold; "worn" if Percentage Used is at least 90; "media_errors" if Media and Data Integrity Errors is greater than zero; "temp_warning_time" if Warning Comp. Temperature Time is greater than zero; "temp_critical_time" if Critical Comp. Temperature Time is greater than zero. Ignore the other fields (including Error Information Log Entries and Unsafe Shutdowns); a missing field never satisfies its condition. Return a sorted list of strings.
tasks.hint: Build a dictionary "field name -> value string", then a small num() function takes the leading digits and commas; bits are (value >> bit) & 1.

tasks.title: The cost of a small RAID write
tasks.statement: Write a function small_write_io(level, n, k): how many disk operations are needed to write k chunks of one stripe of an array of n disks. Return a tuple (reads, writes). raid0: 0 reads, k writes. raid1: 0 reads, n*k writes (each chunk goes to all n mirrors). raid10 with two copies: 0 reads, 2*k writes. raid5 and raid6 (parity count p = 1 and 2; data chunks per stripe d = n - p, 1 <= k <= d): the driver can update the parity in two ways and takes the one with fewer reads. Read-modify-write reads the old data of the chunks being written and the old parity (k + p reads); reconstruct-write reads the chunks of the stripe that are not overwritten (d - k reads). Writes are k + p in both cases (the new data and the new parity). Return the smaller of the two read counts and k + p writes.
tasks.hint: For raid5/6 compute rmw = k + p and rcw = d - k and take the min; writes are always k + p.

tasks.title: Unreadable-sector risk during a rebuild
tasks.statement: A disk returns an unrecoverable read error (URE) with probability 10^(-e) per bit read; spec sheets say "1 in 10^14 bits", which is e = 14. Write a function rebuild_ure_risk(level, n, size_tb, ure_exp): the probability of at least one URE while an array of n disks of size_tb terabytes each (1 TB = 10^12 bytes, 1 byte = 8 bits) recovers after one disk fails. The model: errors are independent, all the data needed for the rebuild is read. raid1 and raid10 read one remaining partner disk; raid5 reads all n-1 remaining disks; raid6 uses the second parity to fix the very first error, so return 0.0 for it; raid0 cannot be rebuilt, return None. The probability is P = 1 - (1 - 10^(-e))^B, where B is the number of bits read; return it rounded to four decimal places (a float). Hint: it is better to compute (1 - q)^B as exp(B * log1p(-q)).
tasks.hint: The number of bits read is B = disks * size_tb * 8e12; P = -expm1(B * log1p(-10**-e)); handle raid6 and raid0 first.

tasks.title: Building mdadm.conf from --detail --scan
tasks.statement: Write a function make_mdadm_conf(scan, mailaddr): scan is the output of mdadm --detail --scan, mailaddr is the address for mail (it may be an empty string). Only lines starting with "ARRAY " are used (comments, INACTIVE-ARRAY and indented continuation lines are skipped). In an ARRAY line the words after the device are properties; words starting with devices= and spares= are dropped, the others stay in the same order. UUID= is required, its value is four groups of eight lowercase hexadecimal digits separated by colons; lines without a valid UUID are skipped. If a UUID was seen already, the repeated line is skipped. Sort the remaining arrays by device name "naturally": cut the name into pieces of digits and non-digits, compare digit pieces as numbers (/dev/md2 before /dev/md10). The result is text: the first line is "DEVICE partitions", the second is "MAILADDR <address>" (only if the address is not empty), then one line "ARRAY <device> <properties separated by spaces>" per array. The text ends with a newline.
tasks.hint: Deduplicate by UUID with a set; the sort key is the list of pieces from re.split(r'(\d+)', dev) with the digit pieces turned into int.

tasks.title: The smartctl exit status
tasks.statement: The smartctl exit status is a bit mask. The bits (from zero): 0 means the command line did not parse; 1 means the device did not open or does not answer; 2 means a SMART command failed or a data checksum is wrong; 3 means the health check returned "disk failing"; 4 means prefailure attributes are at or below the threshold now; 5 means some attributes were at or below the threshold in the past; 6 means the device error log has records; 7 means the self-test log has errors. Write a function smartctl_exit(code): first take code & 255, then return a tuple (severity, list of the numbers of the set bits in ascending order). The severity is "critical" if bit 3 or 4 is set; otherwise "error" if at least one of the bits 0, 1, 2 is set (smartctl could not check the disk); otherwise "warning" if any other bits (5, 6, 7) are set; otherwise "ok".
tasks.hint: The list of bits is [b for b in range(8) if code >> b & 1]; then test the severity in the priority critical, error, warning.
